newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada long-bond yield seen below U.S. soon.
newsitem.headline: Canada long-bond yield seen below U.S. soon.

text.p: Canada's 30-year bond yield is expected to trade below U.S. levels in the near future, bringing the entire Canadian yield curve below the U.S. curve for the first time, analysts said on Tuesday.
The analysts said the phenomenon -- unthinkable just a few years ago -- was further evidence of Canada's growing fiscal and monetary policy credibility.

"It could happen at any minute. There's certainly no economic reason for it not to happen and there's no reason for it not to be sustainable as long as Canada has a favorable balance of payments," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist with High Frequency Economics.
The spread between the Canadian and U.S. 30-year benchmark bond yields fell to a new low of one basis point today, with many traders betting the spread would soon turn negative.
Although estimates varied on when it would happen, most market watchers said it would likely occur within the next several weeks at the latest.

"Whether it happens today or next week we'll have to see. I suspect there will be some resistance, but I think that it's well within the cards," said Michael Gregory, a fixed-income economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers.
Jim Webber, head of fixed-income research with TD Securities, said: "The fundamentals clearly support the idea that Canada will trade through. I think it could happen quite soon."
Canada's yield curve, like that of most countries, has traditionally traded above the U.S. yield curve because investors demanded a higher premium to buy Canadian bonds and T-bills.
That was prompted partly by Canada's higher inflation rate, as well as rising deficits and the risk of Quebec secession.

But last year the traditional relationship changed. With inflation in Canada below U.S. levels and government deficits falling, the Bank of Canada was able to bring Canadian short-term administered rates below U.S. rates.

Canadian fixed-income securities from one month to 10 years were soon trading with lower yields than their U.S. counterparts. Canada's 30-year bond has been the lone exception to the trend, but analysts expected that to change.
